<reason>Side B won by dismantling Side A's economic and supply mechanisms while providing a much more rigorous causal story for how intervention works during the modern synthetic opioid crisis. Side B forced Side A to concede that decriminalizing possession leaves supply illegal, meaning street drugs remain just as toxic and expensive. Furthermore, Side B neutralized Side A's remaining pillars (911 calls and criminal records) early via Good Samaritan laws and drug court expungement—points Side A left largely unanswered until the final closing speech. Finally, Side B resolved Side A's clever pressure question on rational agency by explaining how custodial arrest physically interrupts withdrawal, and defeated Side A's dealer-prosecution defense by pointing out that legalizing possession strips police of the probable cause needed to search for trafficking evidence.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>In [B4.2] and [B4.5], Side B delivered a decisive two-part rebuttal: first answering Side A's trap question on agency by explaining that arrest physically interrupts fentanyl withdrawal rather than relying on long-term rational calculation, and second showing that police cannot prosecute dealers using "scales, cash, communications" [A4.2] when legal possession removes the probable cause required to stop and search suspects in the first place.</best_rebuttal>
